name: Indole-3-carbinol
short: A few animal studies found indole-3-carbinol promoted cancer (most found protection). In a trial in 17 women at high breast-cancer risk, it was well tolerated but raised liver enzyme CYP1A2 activity.
text: The only human study found was small: in a phase I trial in 17 women at high risk of breast cancer, indole-3-carbinol taken by mouth for two 4-week periods at two dose levels was tolerated well by all participants and caused no significant changes in blood estradiol, progesterone, luteinising hormone, follicle-stimulating hormone or sex hormone binding globulin; using caffeine as a probe, the trial found that activity of the liver enzyme CYP1A2 rose in 94% of participants, by 4.1-fold on average, and that NAT-2 activity fell in those whose activity was initially high. The abstract does not discuss effects on medicines. In rats fed indole-3-carbinol for up to 12 months, no significant differences in blood chemistry and no visible or microscopic tissue differences were found between groups, but indole-3-carbinol induced liver CYP enzymes, including CYP1A1, CYP1A2 and CYP3A2. A 1998 review notes that, although most animal studies report inhibitory or protective effects against cancer, a few provide clear evidence that indole-3-carbinol promotes or enhances carcinogenesis, depending on the cancer-causing agent, exposure and species, and advised caution before extensive human trials. No interaction studies with medicines were found in the cited sources.
